items.title: F.P. Journe and Chanel Take Control of Ebel
items.summary: A consortium led by Montres Journe SA, with Chanel and former De Bethune CEO Pierre Jacques, will acquire 95% of Ebel for US$66.5 million. The deal places a historic Swiss marque under owners with considerable independent-watchmaking and luxury-sector expertise.

items.title: Baume & Mercier Extends the Clifton with Five-Day Mechanics
items.summary: The new Clifton 10870 pairs a compact 39mm steel case with the five-day automatic Baumatic calibre, while the 40mm Clifton 10872 adds a perpetual-calendar module. Both limited editions introduce finely patterned ice-blue dials.

items.title: Angelus Returns to Compact, Hand-Wound Chronograph Proportions
items.summary: The Chronographe Tachymètre places Angelus’s hand-wound, column-wheel A5000 calibre inside a 37mm case measuring only 9.25mm thick. Its vintage motoring references, horizontal-clutch architecture and three limited executions reconnect the modern brand with its historic chronographs.

items.title: Nomos Gives the Metro Date Power Reserve the Movement It Needed
items.summary: Nomos updates the Metro Date Power Reserve with the new hand-wound DUW 4701 calibre, finally adding a quick-set date while increasing the power reserve from 42 to 52 hours. The familiar 37mm architecture remains intact and is joined by a new ice-blue dial.

items.title: Armin Strom Carries Rose Gold Through the Entire Tribute³
items.summary: The Tribute³ Au750 uses 18K rose gold across its case, dial and movement bridges, complemented by three distinct hand-executed guilloché patterns. Its manufacture AMW21 calibre is assembled twice and provides a 100-hour power reserve; production is limited to eight pieces.

items.title: Raymond Weil Marks Fifty Years Without Abandoning Accessibility
items.summary: Raymond Weil’s Sydney anniversary event placed the family-owned company’s latest mechanical watches—including the integrated A.R.T collection and a 50-piece Millesime Chronograph—within the wider story of a brand founded during the quartz crisis. Its continued focus on attainable mechanical watchmaking distinguishes it in an industry moving steadily upmarket.

items.title: Toronto Timepiece Show Sharpens Its Focus on Independent Watchmaking
items.summary: The 2026 Toronto Timepiece Show returned with ticketed admission, a dedicated artisanal room and greater emphasis on meaningful interaction between watchmakers and collectors. Its second edition reflects the growing importance of regional fairs as platforms for independent mechanical watchmaking.

items.title: New York’s Autumn Auctions Put Independent Watchmaking in the Spotlight
items.summary: Marteau’s tightly curated “Encore” sale brings together a complete steel F.P. Journe set and work by watchmakers including Sylvain Pinaud and Yosuke Sekiguchi, while Antiquorum returns to New York after more than a decade. Together, the sales offer a revealing view of demand across established and independent mechanical watchmaking.

items.title: Christiaan van der Klaauw Opens the Architecture of Its Mechanical Planetarium
items.summary: The Planetarium Skeleton exposes the movement and world’s smallest mechanical planetarium inside a 40mm platinum case. Limited to six pieces, it turns the Dutch manufacture’s signature astronomical complication into a more architectural and visibly mechanical composition.

items.title: Roger Dubuis Reimagines the Knights of the Round Table
items.summary: Roger Dubuis presents the thirteenth Excalibur Knights of the Round Table, combining twelve sculpted figures with the automatic RD821 calibre in one of the manufacture’s most theatrical mechanical compositions.

items.title: Patek Philippe Turns Milan Into a Celebration of Mechanical Watchmaking
items.summary: Patek Philippe’s largest Watch Art Grand Exhibition brings together historic calibres, rare crafts and new complications, led by a platinum perpetual-calendar chronograph whose calendar indications jump simultaneously in 30 milliseconds.

items.title: Czapek Translates Boris Vian’s Surrealism Into Mechanical Form
items.summary: The 18-piece Promenade L’Écume des Jours combines enamel, mother-of-pearl, jade and miniature painting with Czapek’s micro-rotor Calibre SXH5.1, turning literary inspiration into a richly constructed mechanical watch.

items.title: Omega Gives James Bond’s Seamaster a Hero-and-Villain Pairing
items.summary: Omega introduces two Seamaster Diver 300M editions aligned with James Bond and Spectre, adding distinct 007 cues to the collection’s established mechanical-diver architecture. The pairing extends the cinematic narrative from its familiar hero to the opposing side without abandoning the Seamaster’s professional identity.

items.title: Girard-Perregaux Takes the Laureato Onto the Formula 1 Grid
items.summary: Girard-Perregaux and Williams F1 introduce two 42mm Laureato models with Williams-blue Clous de Paris dials, powered by the automatic GP1800 and GP3300 chronograph calibres. The racing references remain contained within the Laureato’s established architecture rather than overwhelming its mechanical identity.

items.title: King Seiko Makes the Modern VANAC Lighter and More Assertive
items.summary: The new King Seiko VANAC uses a titanium case and bracelet to reduce weight while a fresh dial develops the bold geometry of the 1970s original. Rather than directly reproducing a vintage reference, it continues the more experimental side of King Seiko’s mechanical-watch identity.

items.title: Hamilton Revives the Cushion Watch With Proper Hand-Wound Mechanics
items.summary: Hamilton revives its 1920s cushion watches in compact 30mm and 34mm cases powered by the hand-wound H-42 calibre. Preserving the small proportions and mechanical winding gives the collection more authenticity than a typical vintage-styled revival.

items.title: Longines Sends the Spirit Pilot Collection Into the Blue
items.summary: Longines gives the 39mm Spirit Pilot and Spirit Pilot Flyback matte-blue dials. The Flyback retains a hand-wound, column-wheel flyback chronograph movement, preserving the collection’s legitimate aviation-timing heritage beneath the contemporary colour.

items.title: Cartier Brings the Roadster Back Into the Sports-Watch Conversation
items.summary: After roughly 14 years away, the Cartier Roadster returns in Medium and Large sizes with its tonneau case, automotive dial and signature date magnifier intact. Automatic mechanical movements and 100 metres of water resistance restore it as one of Cartier’s most distinctive sporting designs.

items.title: Patek Philippe Opens a New Chapter for the Perpetual Calendar Chronograph
items.summary: The new Ref. 5978P is only the seventh generation of Patek Philippe’s manually wound perpetual calendar chronograph and the first to combine instantaneous calendar and chronograph-minute mechanisms. Its debut edition uses a 42mm platinum case and is limited to 120 pieces.

items.title: Christopher Ward Revisits Its First In-House Complication
items.summary: The C1 Jump Hour XV marks 15 years since the brand’s first in-house complication with a 39mm case, concentric guilloché dial and JJ01 automatic jump-hour calibre. Its 36-part module stores energy progressively to reduce shock to the escapement at the hour change.

items.title: Bangkok Watch Week Strengthens Southeast Asia’s Watchmaking Platform
items.summary: The second Bangkok Watch Week gathered more than 41 brands and expanded public access through brand forums, vintage watches and mechanical complications. Exhibits from maisons including Bvlgari, Cartier and Blancpain showed the growing regional influence of the event.

items.title: Ulysse Nardin Marks 25 Years of the Freak With Radical Mechanics and Traditional Craft
items.summary: Ulysse Nardin marks 25 years of the Freak with two 99-piece Freak One editions pairing its rotating movement with enamel and guilloché decoration. Both use the automatic UN-240 manufacture calibre, continuing the Freak’s challenge to conventional dials and hands.

items.title: Tudor’s North Flag Legacy Returns to the Center of Its Modern Identity
items.summary: Fratello revisits how the North Flag became Tudor’s first watch with an in-house movement in 2015 and considers why the new Northflag again matters strategically. Its distinctive design and COSC and METAS credentials reinforce Tudor’s independent technical identity.

items.title: Toronto’s Expanding Watch Fair Shows the Strength of Collector-Led Events
items.summary: The third Toronto Timepiece Show gathered roughly 90 brands, including Grönefeld, Christopher Ward, Baltic and Hanhart. Its growth shows how public regional fairs are becoming important meeting points for mechanical-watch brands, independent makers and collectors.

items.title: Gallet’s Return Tests the Swiss Industry’s Mid-Tier Ambitions
items.summary: Backed by Breitling’s House of Brands, Gallet returns with mechanical watches priced from roughly $2,900 to $6,700, including hand-wound B09-powered models. The relaunch is a broader test of whether established Swiss groups can reclaim territory surrendered to value-focused independents and microbrands.

items.title: NOMOS Takes Its Worldtimer Into the Dark
items.summary: The Club Sport Neomatik Worldtimer Dark pairs a black dial and expanded luminous indications with the manufacture’s automatic world-time architecture. It joins the permanent collection as a more nocturnal interpretation of NOMOS’s practical travel watch.

items.title: Panerai Connects a Florentine Centenary to Eight-Day Mechanics
items.summary: Panerai marks 100 years of its historic Florence boutique with an immersive exhibition and two 44mm Luminor Firenze editions. Both use the manually wound P.5000 calibre with an eight-day reserve, translating the maison’s Florentine and naval history into contemporary mechanical watches.

items.title: Louis Vuitton Returns to Its First Watch in Ceramic
items.summary: The Monterey Ceramic revives the pebble-shaped, lugless design of Louis Vuitton’s 1988 watch in 37mm black or green ceramic cases. Its new automatic LFTMA01.02 calibre brings the unconventional form into the permanent collection as a fully mechanical proposition.

items.title: Breguet Reframes the Marine Through Guilloché and Movement Detail
items.summary: The refreshed Marine 5517 and flyback Chronographe 5527 receive solid-gold, hand-guilloché dials, revised displays and subtle movement updates. Available in gold or titanium, the redesign strengthens the collection’s link to Breguet’s historic marine chronometers.

items.title: Hamilton Takes Its Hand-Wound Field Watch Back Into the Game
items.summary: The 38mm Khaki Field Mechanical Modern Warfare 4 edition pairs a compact black-PVD case with Hamilton’s manually wound H-50 calibre and an 80-hour power reserve. Its restrained gaming references preserve the practical character of the underlying mechanical field watch.

items.title: Ulysse Nardin Brings Traditional Craft to the Freak’s Radical Mechanics
items.summary: The new Freak One editions combine the crownless, handless UN-240 carousel movement with blue enamel or hand-guilloché decoration. Limited to 99 pieces each, they place traditional métiers d’art over one of modern mechanical watchmaking’s most unconventional architectures.

items.title: Jaeger-LeCoultre Makes the Power Reserve Part of the Architecture
items.summary: The Master Control Chronometre Date Power Reserve combines a 39mm integrated-bracelet case with the in-house automatic Calibre 738, COSC certification and a 70-hour reserve. Its balanced dial turns a practical indication into a defining visual element.

items.title: Chronoswiss Gives Mechanical Digital Time a Softer Palette
items.summary: The Neo Digiteur Pastel Code presents jumping hours, minutes and seconds through three apertures, powered by the hand-wound C.85757 with a proprietary display module. Mint, Sky and Rose editions soften its architectural case without disguising the unconventional mechanics.

items.title: Circula Enlarges the Facet Without Losing Its Edge
items.summary: The independent German maker expands its angular sports watch to 41mm while retaining the sharply faceted steel case, four dial choices and 68-hour automatic movement.

items.title: Vintage Character Returns to the Market
items.summary: This week’s selection brings together an Omega Ranchero, a discreet Cartier Santos ‘Ghost,’ an Audemars Piguet perpetual calendar and a ZRC Grands Fonds—four very different expressions of collectible mechanical-watch design.

items.title: Glashütte Original Rebuilds the Seventies for the Analogue Era
items.summary: The new 70s collection combines a compact square integrated-bracelet case with record-, amplifier- and hi-fi-inspired dials, powered by the manufacture’s 100-hour automatic Calibre 36.

items.title: Patek Philippe Takes the Celestial Further
items.summary: Patek Philippe’s Celestial Ref. 6105G combines a rotating Geneva sky chart with moon phase, sidereal time, date, and the manufacture’s first wristwatch display for sunrise and sunset. Beneath its unconventional 47mm white-gold form is a technically ambitious evolution of Patek’s astronomical-watch lineage.

items.title: Formex Recasts the Pilot’s Watch in Titanium
items.summary: The AirField Automatic pairs a 40mm hardened Grade 2 titanium case with 150 metres of water resistance and a 65-hour Sellita-based mechanical movement. Its restrained aviation design focuses on legibility, durability, and practical everyday proportions.

items.title: IWC Makes Its Perpetual Calendar Easier to Set
items.summary: The Big Pilot’s Watch Perpetual Calendar ProSet ‘Le Petit Prince’ develops Kurt Klaus’s mechanically programmed calendar with IWC’s newer ProSet adjustment system. It preserves the complication’s synchronized displays while making correction and long-term ownership more approachable.

items.title: Héron Builds a Compact Explorer for Everyday Use
items.summary: Canadian independent Héron introduces the Continental, reworking explorer-watch language through a 37mm hardened-steel case and luminous sandwich dial. A Miyota 9039 automatic movement and beads-of-rice bracelet turn its vintage references into an approachable daily mechanical watch.

items.title: A. Lange & Söhne Brings Two New Watches to the Concours Lawn
items.summary: A. Lange & Söhne presented new versions of the 1815 UP/DOWN and platinum Triple Split at the Concours of Elegance at Hampton Court. By placing complex mechanical watches within classic-car culture, the brand reinforces a shared language of engineering, craft and longevity.

items.title: FounderFest Takes Independent Releases from Event to Global Window
items.summary: FounderFest’s seven independent-watch collaborations entered a 24-hour global ordering window before returning to in-store exclusivity in London, New York and Melbourne. The format connects a physical collector event with limited worldwide access, offering smaller makers an alternative release model.

items.title: Baume & Mercier Gives the Clifton a Cooler Mechanical Register
items.summary: Baume & Mercier gives the 39mm Clifton Automatic Date an ice-blue guilloché dial while retaining the poised proportions of a 1950s dress watch. The Baumatic manufacture movement brings a five-day power reserve, making the new tone more than a surface change.

items.title: Panerai Makes a Proper 42mm Luminor
items.summary: Panerai brings full tool-watch capability to a 42mm Luminor for the first time, retaining 500m water resistance and its signature crown-protection bridge. The three references use the automatic P.980 with a three-day reserve, proving smaller dimensions need not compromise capability.

items.title: Venezianico Turns Lightness into an Italian Mechanical Statement
items.summary: At 48 grams, the Venezianico Redentore Levius reframes a dress watch through a titanium case and hand-turned guilloché dial. Its manual-wind V5000 is designed and made in Italy, turning the release into a concrete step toward a stronger domestic mechanical-watchmaking base.

items.title: Bianchet Brings a New Ceramic Contrast to the UltraFino Skeleton
items.summary: Bianchet’s Tonneau UltraFino Ceramic Skeleton pairs deep-blue and white ceramic with an exposed ultra-thin mechanical architecture. The contrast reinforces the growing space for lightweight, sporty haute horlogerie.

items.title: Jaeger-LeCoultre Finds Clarity in the Master Control Chronometre
items.summary: Jaeger-LeCoultre refines its classic date watch through a 38mm case, 8.4mm profile and integrated bracelet. Inside, the automatic Calibre 899 provides a 70-hour reserve and the technical foundation for a more restrained daily proposition.

items.title: Dublin’s Chronography Gives Independent Watchmaking a New Stage
items.summary: Chronography brings independent and microbrand watchmaking into a focused one-day event for Irish collectors. Its format shows how smaller physical fairs can become meaningful discovery and sales channels beyond the traditional European circuit.

items.title: Christopher Ward Puts Mechanical Chronographs Back in the Sealander
items.summary: Christopher Ward returns to the mechanical chronograph with the C63 Sealander, ending a gap in non-quartz chronographs since 2020. Its Sellita SW510-1 automatic movement and 56-hour reserve bring complication back to the brand’s core price territory.

items.title: Tutima Balances Titanium with Gold, and Hand-Wound Tradition
items.summary: Tutima’s new Patria pairs a grade-five titanium case with 18K gold details and its hand-wound Calibre 617. A 60-hour reserve and Glashütte finishing keep the material contrast rooted in the movement.

items.title: FounderFest Makes Independent Watchmaking a Live Stage
items.summary: Time+Tide’s FounderFest brings independent makers, collectors and live music together across New York, London and Melbourne. The associated mechanical watch collaborations turn the release calendar into a more communal, in-person format.

items.title: Studio Underd0g brings a monopusher chronograph to Dubai.
items.summary: Studio Underd0g and Ahmed Seddiqi introduce the 100-piece Chan3ad with Eastern Arabic numerals and a two-layer fish-inspired dial. At its core is the manually wound Sellita SW510 M monopusher chronograph movement with 63 hours of power reserve.

items.title: Parmigiani lets the calibre carry the colour.
items.summary: Parmigiani Fleurier presents the 30-piece Tonda PF Skeleton in rose gold and Milano Blue. The openworked automatic PF777 movement, with twin barrels, finishing and structural depth, becomes the watch’s true visual centre.

items.title: Czapek turns a novel into a mechanical dial.
items.summary: Czapek’s Promenade L’Écume des Jours translates Boris Vian’s pianocktail and water-lily imagery into Grand Feu enamel, hand-painted details and the automatic SXH5.1 micro-rotor movement. The edition is limited to 18 pieces.

items.title: Watches and Wonders expands its independent horizon.
items.summary: Watches and Wonders 2027 will expand to 75 exhibiting brands, with Berneron, Singer Reimagined and Porsche Design among the first-time participants. The growth gives independent mechanical watchmaking a more formal and concentrated international stage.

items.title: Glashütte Original finds a mechanical rhythm in the seventies.
items.summary: Glashütte Original’s new The 70s line draws on vinyl, hi-fi and 1970s design, while remaining anchored by the manufacture Calibre 36 automatic movement, its 100-hour power reserve and traditional Saxon finishing.

items.title: Neode begins with architecture, not decoration.
items.summary: New independent brand Neode launches its N01 First Edition with a Voutilainen-made case, a deeply reworked manual Chronode movement and an eight-day power reserve. Limited to 25 pieces, it puts structure, proportion and movement architecture ahead of ornament.

items.title: Singer Reimagined makes GMT a matter of architecture.
items.summary: Singer’s 1970 DualTrack places dual-time reading inside a slimmer 1970s-inspired integrated-bracelet case. Its manual-winding ST5001 movement uses four barrels to deliver six days of power reserve.

items.title: Louis Moinet turns lunar time into a mechanical landscape.
items.summary: Moon Meteor combines miniature painting, meteorite material and a high-precision moon-phase display in a 12-piece titanium edition. Its automatic LM113 movement drives a lunar cycle claimed accurate to one day in 122 years.

items.title: Straum gives its integrated-bracelet formula an outdoor life.
items.summary: Norwegian independent Straum takes its integrated-bracelet design into more capable territory with titanium, 100m water resistance and stronger lume. The Expedition retains the automatic La Joux-Perret G100 movement with a 68-hour power reserve.

items.title: Rolex reopens the calendar conversation.
items.summary: Rolex revisits the historic Padellone with a new Perpetual model featuring an instantaneous annual calendar and moonphase. It brings a more complicated proposition back into the brand’s dress-watch narrative.

items.title: TAG Heuer makes the Carrera Sport more wearable.
items.summary: The new Carrera Chronograph Sport shrinks from 44mm to 42mm while retaining the TH20-00 automatic column-wheel chronograph and its 80-hour power reserve. It is a mechanical update shaped as much by daily proportions as by racing credentials.

items.title: Complications take the stage in New York.
items.summary: WatchTime New York will bring minute repeaters, perpetual calendars and tourbillons to the foreground this October. The programme shows how technical watchmaking and independent brands are becoming central to the fair’s proposition.

items.title: Serena Williams Reframes the Royal Oak Chronograph
items.summary: Audemars Piguet’s 38mm Royal Oak Selfwinding Chronograph for Serena Williams pairs white ceramic with a pink mother-of-pearl dial. Its integrated, column-wheel Calibre 6401 keeps the 500-piece edition firmly rooted in mechanical watchmaking.

items.title: Six Omega Stopwatches Preserve a Lost Racing Circuit
items.summary: A fitted set of six Omega professional mechanical stopwatches, engraved LEVIN M.R.C., preserves a direct link to a vanished New Zealand racing circuit. The objects show how mechanical timing equipment once formed part of motorsport’s working infrastructure.

items.title: Rolex Turns Four Daytonas into a Seasonal Charity Series
items.summary: Rolex created four unique Cosmograph Daytonas around the seasons, combining precious metals, natural-stone dials and gem setting. Powered by the automatic Calibre 4131, the watches will be auctioned by Phillips to benefit two charitable organisations.

items.title: De Bethune rejects scarcity as a shortcut to desire.
items.summary: New CEO Antoine Pin says the brand will not treat limited production or secondary-market appreciation as its central proposition, instead building demand through art, innovation and long-term product value. It is a clear challenge to the idea that rarity alone creates desirability.

items.title: Cartier brings the Roadster back without making it a museum piece.
items.summary: Cartier’s Roadster revival updates the early sports-watch design with the maison’s current quick-change strap system. The point is not simply a reissue, but to bring an overlooked line back into the brand’s present-day product language.

items.title: Citizen turns fifty years of Eco-Drive into two atmospheric ATTESA watches.
items.summary: Citizen marks Eco-Drive’s fiftieth anniversary with Green Flash and Purple Aurora ATTESA limited editions, each capped at 1,500 pieces. Structural colour film and vapour deposition create the light effects, while the F950 movement provides rapid satellite-signal reception.

items.title: Rolex still leads, but secondary-market attention is spreading.
items.summary: Chrono24’s new report shows Rolex remains the largest brand on its platform, but has lost share in every major price segment since 2023 as Cartier, Patek Philippe, Audemars Piguet and Vacheron Constantin gain ground. The pandemic-era Rolex premium has also largely unwound.

items.title: Tudor’s Northflag returns with a sharper identity.
items.summary: The new Northflag continues Tudor’s tool-watch line while adding GMT functionality and a more complete contemporary specification. It shows the brand using historical threads to strengthen its range beyond anniversary-led storytelling.

items.title: Ebel’s 115th anniversary makes room for both mechanics and jewellery.
items.summary: Ebel marks 115 years with two limited Sport Classic watches: a Dubois Dépraz automatic chronograph and a gemstone-set quartz model. Together they make a direct case for the brand’s old idea that function and beauty can serve distinct collectors in parallel.

items.title: Swiss watchmakers face a price-and-value reality check.
items.summary: Deloitte’s survey of 6,500 consumers across 13 markets suggests buyers put price-to-value ahead of the industry’s constant flow of novelties. It also highlights a growing mismatch between brands’ focus on mono-brand boutiques and customers’ preference for choice and comparison.

items.title: Bangkok Watch Week signals Southeast Asia’s growing horological pull.
items.summary: The second Siam Paragon Bangkok Watch Week will run September 22–27 with more than 45 participating brands—more than double the first edition. Its growth shows how watch fairs are increasingly reaching toward collector communities beyond the traditional European circuit.

items.title: A. Lange & Söhne pairs new complications with the world of classic cars.
items.summary: At Hampton Court Palace’s Concours of Elegance, Lange presented the new platinum Triple Split and two 1815 Up/Down special editions. For a small high-watchmaking house, the event shows how cultural settings can frame craft and heritage more effectively than a standalone launch.

items.title: WatchPro USA names the people and businesses shaping the American watch market.
items.summary: The 2026 WatchPro USA Awards recognised achievement across retail, brand building, customer experience and industry leadership—not merely new releases. Its winners offer a useful snapshot of the businesses and people setting the pace in a growing American watch market.

items.title: Jaeger-LeCoultre brings fifteen complications into one Grande Sonnerie.
items.summary: Jaeger-LeCoultre’s one-off Duomètre Grande Complication à Grande Sonnerie unites a Westminster-style grande sonnerie, minute repeater, perpetual calendar and flying tourbillon in Calibre 182. It is a forceful reminder that extreme mechanical watchmaking remains central to the maison’s identity.

items.title: Panerai marks a century in Florence with an eight-day Luminor.
items.summary: For the centenary of its historic Florence boutique, Panerai revisits a 1960s reference in the limited Luminor Firenze 8 Giorni PAM01794. The release uses the brand’s familiar eight-day hand-wound movement to connect its modern identity with its Florentine origins.

items.title: Gérald Genta returns to the minute repeater with restraint.
items.summary: The revived maison’s Geneva Minute Repeater Golden Obsidian pairs a 40mm yellow-gold cushion case with a natural golden-obsidian dial, at roughly 9.6mm thick. It continues the LVMH-backed revival through thin dress watches and serious complications rather than a rapid expansion of references.

items.title: Legare revives an overlooked double-balance idea.
items.summary: The new independent brand’s Chapter I AGP Inverted draws on Albert-Gustave Piguet’s 1932 double-balance chronometer project. Its inverted LC1-AGP-01 movement makes the mechanism the visual centre, showing a different route to distinction than another conventional tourbillon.

items.title: Timex brings the premium GMT down to 38mm.
items.summary: Timex’s Atelier GMT Première M1a reduces the collection to a 38mm case while retaining a Swiss movement and double-domed sapphire crystal. It is a useful sign that the smaller-case trend is reaching a genuinely broad consumer brand, not only high-end houses.

items.title: King Seiko lets Tokyo enter the dial.
items.summary: King Seiko’s new steel Vanac HKF005 uses a dark, speckled dial to evoke Tokyo’s night skyline. It is a regular-production release—not another scarcity exercise—and shows how a familiar sports-watch format can gain character through surface rather than complication.

items.title: Breitling turns a Miles Davis tribute into a collecting proposition.
items.summary: The 500-piece Navitimer B09 Miles Davis draws on the musician’s ref. 806, with a hand-wound chronograph and a reworked Air Racer bracelet. More tellingly, the 50-set top tier includes entry to Breitling’s forthcoming Social Club—an increasingly experiential approach to ownership.

items.title: Awake makes lacquer the point, not the decoration.
items.summary: Awake’s new Son Mai Frosted Leaf colours continue its use of Vietnamese lacquer, natural pigments and silver leaf, with roughly 15 hours of work in each dial. At around 100 pieces per colour each year, it is a useful example of an independent brand building distinction through craft at a relatively accessible level.

items.title: Nomos turns its dials into an atelier
items.summary: Nomos’s made-to-order Twice Unique collection treats five familiar models as canvases for nine artist-led dial designs. Each commission pairs a steel watch with an 18K gold counterpart, favouring handwork and individuality over conventional limited-edition logic.

items.title: The GPHG finalists set the stage for November
items.summary: The 2026 GPHG finalists are now public ahead of the November 7 ceremony. Revised, non-gendered categories and a new jury president signal an awards institution seeking a broader global audience—while giving smaller brands a meaningful stage.

items.title: Rolex sends four unique Daytonas to charity auction
items.summary: Four one-off, season-inspired gem-set Daytonas will be sold separately by Phillips in London on September 28. The proceeds support the Federer Foundation and Re:wild, placing a rare public Rolex project at the intersection of craftsmanship and philanthropy.

items.title: Geneva Watch Days signals a renewed search for volume
items.summary: With 71 brands and nearly 400 new watches, the fair pointed to smaller cases, bolder design and renewed interest in more attainable price points—an industry response to shrinking unit sales and younger buyers.

items.title: Hermès’s watchmaking ambitions meet a perception problem
items.summary: After two decades of investment, Hermès is building real watchmaking scale. Yet its association with Birkin access and weaker resale values shows that technical capability alone does not create collector confidence.

items.title: Watch fairs multiply as the industry looks for new audiences
items.summary: Geneva Watch Days continues to grow, new collector-led fairs are emerging in the US, and MCH Group is preparing Basilia for 2027. Physical shows are becoming places for brands, media and communities to meet—not merely order-taking events.
